title: You didn’t call it rebellion.
paragraphs: You didn’t call it rebellion.
You called it fairness.
That’s how it started for Absalom.
Not with a sword in his hand—but with sympathy in his voice.
He stood at the city gate, where broken people came looking for justice. People with disputes. People who felt unheard. People who believed the system had failed them.
And Absalom leaned in close.
“If only I were appointed judge in the land… then everyone who has a complaint or case could come to me and I would see that they receive justice.” —2 Samuel 15:4
It sounded righteous.
It felt right.
But here’s what most people don’t realize…
He wasn’t building justice.
He was building a throne.
“Also, whenever anyone approached him to bow down before him, Absalom would reach out his hand, take hold of him and kiss him… So he stole the hearts of the people of Israel.” —2 Samuel 15:5–6
Read that again.
He stole their hearts.
Not earned.
Not given.
Stolen.
And you don’t steal hearts unless you’re trying to replace someone.
In this case—his own father, King David.
This is where it stops being a political story and becomes a spiritual mirror.
Because you’ve seen this before.
Not in a palace.
In your own thoughts.
That subtle voice that says, “I would do better.”
That quiet resentment when authority doesn’t meet your expectations.
That inner courtroom where you sit as judge… jury… and replacement.
God saw it.
You knew.
Absalom didn’t start with open rebellion. He started with wounded pride, unhealed offense, and a hunger to be seen as right.
And instead of bringing it to God…
He weaponized it.
“After four years, Absalom said to the king… ‘Let me go to Hebron and fulfill a vow I made to the Lord.’” —2 Samuel 15:7–8
Even his rebellion wore religious language.
Let that land.
He used the name of God to cover a plan that was never submitted to God.
How many times has that happened in quieter ways?
Serving… but needing recognition.
Speaking truth… but fueled by pride.
Calling out wrong… but secretly wanting position.
This is how deception works.
It doesn’t show up as evil.
It shows up as justified.
But Scripture cuts through it:
“The heart is deceitful above all things and beyond cure. Who can understand it?” —Jeremiah 17:9
Absalom believed he was the answer.
That’s why he never saw himself as the problem.
And that is the most dangerous place a soul can stand.
Because once you believe your rebellion is righteousness…
You stop repenting.
The story doesn’t end at the gate.
It ends in a field.
Fleeing.
Exposed.
Alone.
“As Absalom was riding his mule… his head got caught in the thick branches of a large oak tree. He was left hanging in midair…” —2 Samuel 18:9
The same man who lifted himself above authority…
Now hangs helpless between heaven and earth.
Suspended.
Powerless.
Judged.
Sin always promises elevation.
But it delivers exposure.
And here is the weight of it all…
David, the king he betrayed, didn’t celebrate his fall.
He wept.
“O my son Absalom! My son, my son Absalom! If only I had died instead of you…” —2 Samuel 18:33
That’s not just a father grieving.
That’s a shadow of something deeper.
Because centuries later, another Son would come.
Not to steal hearts—
But to redeem them.
Not to take a throne by manipulation—
But to carry a cross in surrender.
Jesus Christ didn’t disguise His mission.
He exposed sin, called for repentance, and offered grace.
“For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” —Luke 19:10
Where Absalom built loyalty through deception…
Jesus builds transformation through truth.
Where Absalom took what wasn’t his…
Jesus gave what didn’t have to be given—His life.
This is where everything turns.
Because the same heart that drove Absalom can still live in you.
The need to be right.
The hunger to be seen.
The quiet rebellion dressed as justice.
But there’s another way.
“God opposes the proud but shows favor to the humble.” —James 4:6
You don’t have to hang where Absalom fell.
You can kneel where grace begins.
Repentance isn’t weakness.
It’s clarity.
It’s finally calling sin what it is—without disguise.
And trusting that Jesus already paid for it.
Originally written by Gospel Warrior.

There are deeper layers to this—patterns in Scripture, warnings most people ignore, and truths that expose what we hide well. Not surface inspiration, but confrontation that leads to real transformation.
Say it plainly.
“I’ve been calling it justice, but it’s pride.”
Let that be your first honest sentence.
